newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Air Afrique board sets balanced budget for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Air Afrique board sets balanced budget for 1997.

text.p: The board of multinational carrier Air Afrique has belatedly set a balanced budget for 1997 and plans costs cuts to achieve that, a spokesman for the company said on Wednesday.

Managing director Sir Harry Tirvengadum took over the reins of the troubled airline in February this year and rejected the budget drawn up by the previous administration, which saw a deficit of 13 billion CFA francs ($21 million) for 1997.
"The new plan sees a balanced budget, with a reduction in costs and a concentration of activity on air transport," the spokesman said after a board meeting that ended late on Tuesday.
Ancillary activities, such as certain interests in the tourist sector, are being discarded.

There has also been a review of air services. The company is trying to put the accent on more profitable journeys, although the spokesman said it was obliged to balance profitability and the public service nature of the airline.
No services are being cut completely, but the number of flights serving some destinations is being reduced.
The company is owned by the governments of Benin, Burkina Faso, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Ivory Coast, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Senegal and Togo. Air France also has a small stake.
The airline's owner governments have put together a plan to solve Air Afrique's crippling debt problem which involves setting up a leasing company to take over its planes and debts.
The spokesman said the group's total debt currently stood at 181 billion CFA francs, reduced from 200 billion by various payments this year.
Much of the debt was contracted to buy planes in the early 1990s, but Air Afrique hit serious repayment problems after the 50 percent devaluation of the CFA franc in January 1994.
A large part of its revenue is denominated in CFA francs, the currency of 15 African states in the Franc Zone, including all of Air Afrique's member states except Mauritania.

The spokesman said the debt restructuring plan would be the subject of a special meeting in Paris on Thursday involving Air Afrique shareholders and ASECNA, the air safety agency covering francophone Africa.

ASECNA has agreed to put some of its surplus funds into the proposed leasing company, which would be in a position to make regular payments to creditors, but it has sought a three percent interest payment on the capital employed.

The spokesman said it was seeking other guarantees, for example that insurance companies should no longer have the right to seize the Air Afrique planes after ownership is transferred from the airline to the leasing company.
He noted that the annual meeting of ASECNA in Madagascar at the end of June had passed a resolution calling for a rapid conclusion of the Air Afrique deal. -- Abidjan newsroom +225 21 90 90
